title: "Choose an analysis"
description: >
  A decision guide: four questions about your data that lead to one of the
  eight functions, a table of common situations, and what each function is
  for.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

The eight functions share one calling convention and return the same kind of
object, so the choice between them depends only on your data: what the
outcome is, how the observations are related, and what you need to adjust
for. Each function below links to a walkthrough that runs it on real data.

## Four questions

Answer these in order and stop at the first one that settles it.

1. Is the outcome binary, a count, or another non-continuous measurement?

   | Outcome | Function |
   |---|---|
   | Two categories (yes/no, success/failure, 0/1) | `anova_bin()` |
   | A count of events (0, 1, 2, ...), possibly over differing exposure time | `anova_count()` |
   | A proportion out of a known number of trials, a positive right-skewed measurement (costs, times), or anything else with a GLM family | `anova_glm()` |
   | A continuous measurement | go to question 2 |

2. Are the same subjects measured more than once (before and after, at
   several time points, under several conditions)? If yes, use `anova_rm()`.

3. Are there several continuous outcomes to analyse together? If yes, use
   `anova_manova()`.

4. Is there a numeric covariate to adjust for (a baseline score, age, a
   pre-treatment measurement)? If yes, use `anova_ancova()`. If no, use
   `anova_welch()`, or `anova_kw()` when the outcome is ordinal or so skewed
   that a mean is not a useful summary.

## Common situations

| You have | Use | Not |
|---|---|---|
| Three or more groups, variances look different | `anova_welch()` | a classical ANOVA, which assumes equal variances |
| Two groups | `anova_welch()` (it is Welch's t test) | a pooled t test |
| Ratings on a 1–5 scale | `anova_kw()` | a comparison of means of ordinal codes |
| A baseline and a follow-up score, randomised groups | `anova_ancova()` with the baseline as covariate | change scores |
| The same people at three time points | `anova_rm()` | an ANOVA that treats each measurement as a new person |
| Height, weight and waist size on the same people | `anova_manova()` | three separate ANOVAs with no joint test |
| Two crossed factors and a continuous outcome | `anova_glm()` with `interaction = TRUE` | `anova_welch()`, which cannot separate main effects from the interaction |
| Passed / failed | `anova_bin()` | a comparison of 0/1 means |
| Number of visits over different lengths of follow-up | `anova_count()` with `offset` | counts per person ignoring exposure |
| Successes out of a known number of trials | `anova_glm()` with `family = "binomial"` and the trials as `weights` | percentages analysed as continuous |
| Costs or durations, positive and skewed | `anova_glm()` with `family = Gamma(link = "log")` | a log transformation, when you want means on the original scale |

## One outcome, independent groups

### `anova_welch()`

Welch's test compares group means without assuming equal variances. When the
variances are equal it gives almost the same answer as the classical F test.
When they are not, the classical test can be badly wrong, most of all when
the smallest group has the largest variance. That makes it the default for
comparing means. The [walkthrough](welch.html) runs it on data with unequal
group variances.

### `anova_kw()`

The Kruskal-Wallis test compares the groups' rank distributions, with Dunn's
test for the pairwise comparisons. Use it for ordinal outcomes (convert an
ordered factor with `as.integer()` first), for heavy-tailed or very skewed
data in small samples, or when outliers are real values you cannot drop. It
asks whether values in one group tend to be larger than in another, which is
a different question from whether the means differ, and the
[Kruskal-Wallis walkthrough](kruskal-wallis.html) shows how to read it.

### `anova_ancova()`

When a numeric variable measured before treatment (a baseline score, age,
weight) predicts the outcome, adjusting for it removes that part of the
variation and makes the group comparison more precise. In a randomised study
it is the right way to use a baseline measurement: better than analysing
change scores, and better than ignoring the baseline. The
[ANCOVA walkthrough](ancova.html) covers covariate centring, the
homogeneity-of-slopes test and when to fix the model in advance.

## Repeated measures and several outcomes

### `anova_rm()`

When each subject contributes several measurements, the measurements are
correlated. Treating them as independent observations overstates the sample
size and makes every p-value too small. `anova_rm()` fits the
repeated-measures ANOVA through `afex`, with within-subject factors
(`within`), between-subject factors (`between`), the Greenhouse-Geisser or
Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity, and generalised eta squared. Subjects
missing a cell are removed and listed in `$subjects_dropped`. The
[repeated-measures walkthrough](repeated-measures.html) runs a mixed design.

With one pre-treatment and one post-treatment measurement and randomised
groups, an ANCOVA of the post score adjusting for the pre score usually has
more power than the repeated-measures analysis of the same data. It also
answers the question most such studies ask: did the groups differ after
treatment, given where they started?

### `anova_manova()`

Use a MANOVA when the outcomes are one construct measured several ways, or
when you want one test that controls the error rate across them before
looking at each. It uses the correlations between the outcomes, which
separate ANOVAs ignore, and then follows up each outcome on its own. With
covariates it becomes a MANCOVA. The [MANOVA walkthrough](manova.html)
covers the four test statistics, the canonical discriminant analysis, and
what to do when Box's M rejects.

## Binary, count and other outcomes

### `anova_bin()`

`anova_bin()` fits a logistic regression and reports it as an analysis of
deviance, with odds ratios, marginal probabilities and pairwise
comparisons. It detects separation (a group in which every outcome is the
same), which makes ordinary intervals meaningless, and says so in `$notes`. Aggregated data, one row per group and
outcome with a count, go in through `weights`, as the
[binary-outcomes walkthrough](binary.html) shows.

### `anova_count()`

`anova_count()` fits a Poisson model when the counts are no more variable
than a Poisson distribution allows, and a negative binomial model when the
Pearson dispersion is above `overdispersion_threshold` (1.5 by default).
Set `model` to choose the family yourself. When units were observed for different
lengths of time or at different sizes, give the exposure as `offset` and the
results become rates. The [counts walkthrough](counts.html) models insurance
claims per policy holder this way.

### `anova_glm()`

Any `stats::family`: Gamma or inverse Gaussian for positive, right-skewed
measurements; binomial with trial weights for proportions; quasi families
when the variance does not follow the family's rule. With the default
Gaussian family it is the classical ANOVA with Type II or Type III sums of
squares. The [GLM walkthrough](glm.html) fits a Gamma model to car prices.

## Several grouping variables

Every function accepts several grouping columns. `anova_welch()` and
`anova_kw()` combine them into one factor of the cells that contain data, so
they test the cells and cannot separate main effects from an interaction.
`anova_ancova()`, `anova_manova()`, `anova_bin()`, `anova_count()` and
`anova_glm()` fit them as factors, with or without their interaction
(`interaction`), and with Type II or Type III tests (`type`). For a classical
two-way ANOVA of a continuous outcome, use `anova_glm()` with its default
Gaussian family:

```{r twoway}
tg <- transform(ToothGrowth, dose = factor(dose))
anova_glm(tg, "len", c("supp", "dose"), interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)$anova
```

The [GLM walkthrough](glm.html) runs a two-way ANOVA and explains the choice
between Type II and Type III.
